subject: Pathology
summary: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic, immune‑mediated disease of the intra‑ and extra‑hepatic bile ducts that leads to progressive fibrosis and beading on imaging. It is strongly linked to ulcerative colitis and presents with cholestatic liver enzyme elevation and pruritus.

sections.p: PSC is defined by chronic inflammation, obliterative fibrosis, and segmental dilation of bile ducts, producing a characteristic beaded appearance on cholangiography. Diagnosis requires a cholestatic pattern of liver enzymes, imaging evidence of ductal irregularity, and exclusion of other cholestatic diseases.
b: Beaded ducts on MRCP or ERCP

t.b: Is the patient cholestatic? ↑ALP suggests cholestasis.
Confirms cholestasis; ↑γ‑GT supports bile duct injury.
Shows beaded ducts; confirms PSC when combined with labs.
Rules out autoimmune hepatitis; negative in most PSC.
Excludes viral hepatitis as cause of cholestasis.

sections.p: The Mayo Risk Score and the Mayo Clinic staging system stratify prognosis based on bilirubin, albumin, INR, and variceal bleeding history. Early stages have normal bilirubin; advanced stages show cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
b: Mayo Risk Score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, varices)

sections.p: PSC’s exact cause is unknown, but it is considered an autoimmune process often triggered by gut‑liver axis dysregulation. The strongest association is with ulcerative colitis.

Patients report fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice. Physical exam may reveal scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension. Extra‑intestinal manifestations include uveitis and inflammatory arthritis.
A stepwise work‑up confirms cholestasis, excludes mimics, and assesses liver damage. In low‑resource settings, basic biochemistry and ultrasound can guide further testing.

t.b: Is the patient jaundiced? ↑Total bilirubin indicates cholestasis.
Detects biliary dilation and liver parenchyma; useful when MRCP unavailable.
Assesses synthetic function; low albumin predicts cirrhosis.
Evaluates clotting; prolonged INR suggests advanced liver disease.
Provides definitive ductal imaging and allows therapeutic intervention if needed.

sections.p: PSC can progress to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, cholangiocarcinoma, and liver failure. Sudden worsening of jaundice, ascites, or encephalopathy warrants urgent care.

No disease‑modifying therapy exists; management focuses on treating associated ulcerative colitis, preventing complications, and monitoring for cholangiocarcinoma. Ursodeoxycholic acid may improve liver enzymes but does not alter prognosis.
b: Infliximab or azathioprine for active UC

sections.p: Patients require yearly liver function tests, imaging, and colonoscopy. Lifestyle measures include avoiding hepatotoxic drugs and maintaining a healthy diet.
Other cholestatic liver diseases such as primary biliary cholangitis, drug‑induced cholestasis, and viral hepatitis can mimic PSC.
Serum ALP can be elevated in bone disease; γ‑GT may be normal in early PSC. Imaging may miss early ductal changes if low‑resolution modalities are used.
b: Early PSC may have normal γ‑GT

faq.a: Most cases are sporadic; a small percentage may have a family history, but no clear inheritance pattern.
There is no cure; treatment focuses on managing complications and monitoring for cancer.

faq.q: Does PSC always cause liver failure?
faq.a: Many patients remain asymptomatic for years; only a subset progress to cirrhosis or liver failure.

exam: Explain why ulcerative colitis is the most common associated disease with PSC.
Describe the imaging findings that differentiate PSC from primary biliary cholangitis.
Outline the surveillance strategy for cholangiocarcinoma in a patient with PSC.
